title: Piston-Like Information Engine II: Boundary-Controlled Optimum in Active Matter
authors: Laura Hoek, Neta Ben Ari, Rémi Goerlich, Saar Rahav, Yael Roichman
abstract: Information engines convert information into extractable work through measurements and feedback. We realize an engine that employs information to compress a gas of self-propelled bristle bots. Its work per measurement, $\bar{W}$, is controlled by the size of the detection region $Δx$ and the probability $p_1$ that this region is vacant. In thermal systems, $\bar{W}$ follows the universal form $-p_1 \ln p_1$, whereas the active engine shows a qualitatively modified relation. As particle density increases, the maximum of $\bar{W}(Δx)$ switches between two distinct operating regimes. Notably, this transition is also found in the solutions that maximize power output for finite-time cycles with dynamics affected by dry friction. We attribute this nonequilibrium feature to the accumulation of active particles near the boundaries.
summary: This work develops and experimentally tests an information engine using active bristle bots to convert information into mechanical work. The study finds that the work output deviates significantly from predictions based on ideal thermal systems. Crucially, the optimal operating regime switches based on particle density, a feature confirmed even when considering realistic friction and finite-time cycle dynamics.
main_problem: The paper investigates information engines that extract work from active matter, comparing their performance to theoretical thermal systems.
main_result: The active engine exhibits a qualitatively modified work-information relationship compared to thermal systems, and the optimal operating regime switches depending on particle density.
method: The work is calculated by analyzing the mean work extracted ($ ar{W} = p_1 W_{st}$) based on the probability of finding an empty detection region ($p_1$) during a piston-like cycle.
model_or_system: The system uses self-propelled bristle bots (active matter) confined in a box, where work is extracted by periodically measuring the occupancy of a movable detection region near a piston.
key_observables: Mean work per measurement ($ ar{W}$), empty-region probability ($p_1$), and maximum power output ($	ilde{P}$).
important_parameters: Particle density ($\Phi$), detection region size ($\Delta x$), and the energy scale ($	ilde{\alpha}$ vs. $k_B T$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the active particle force scales linearly with density ($\alpha \Phi$), and later models incorporate dry friction and finite-time cycle constraints.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, pressure scaling ($P \propto \Phi$), comparisons of $ ar{W}$ vs $p_1$ showing regime switches, and simulations of stick-slip dynamics under friction.
paper_structure: The paper moves from defining the information engine concept and measuring work in active matter, to comparing results against ideal gas theory, analyzing the density-dependent switching of optimal operation, and finally modeling the cycle under realistic, non-ideal friction constraints.
why_interesting: The work done here on active matter thermodynamics and non-equilibrium work extraction provides a physical realization of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics far from equilibrium, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems and energy transduction.
